'''Helena Chmura Kraemer''' is an American professor emerita of [[biostatistics]] at [[Stanford University]]. She is known for her work on improving research methodologies, particularly in evaluating measurement reliability, detecting and correcting errors, and optimizing statistical power in studies where biological and behavioral factors intersect. Kraemer is a fellow of the [[American Statistical Association]].

== Education ==
Kraemer completed a Bachelor of Arts in mathematics with [[Phi Beta Kappa]] honors from [[Smith College]] in 1957.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/author/helena-chmura-kraemer|title=Kraemer, Helena|date=2018-09-12|work=SAGE Publications Inc|access-date=2018-09-20|language=en-us}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite news|url=http://newsletter.blogs.wesleyan.edu/2014/05/25/honorarydegrees2014/|title=Wesleyan Confers Honorary Degrees on White, Shaw '76, Kraemer|last=Drake|first=Olivia|date=2014-05-25|work=News @ Wesleyan|access-date=2018-09-20|language=en-us}}</ref> In 1958, she attended [[University of Manchester]] as a [[Fulbright fellow]]. Kraemer earned a Doctor of Philosophy in statistics from [[Stanford University]] in 1963.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://profiles.stanford.edu/helena-kraemer|title=Helena Chmura Kraemer's Profile|website=Stanford University|language=en|access-date=2018-09-20}}</ref> Her dissertation was titled ''Point Estimation in Learning Models''. Her [[doctoral advisor]] was [[Patrick Suppes]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kraemer|first=Helena Chmura|date=1964|title=Point estimation in learning models|journal=Journal of Mathematical Psychology|language=en|volume=1|issue=1|pages=28–53|doi=10.1016/0022-2496(64)90016-1|issn=0022-2496}}</ref>

== Career ==
Kraemer is a professor emerita of biostatistics in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at Stanford University.<ref name=":1" /> She researches the intersection of biological and behavioral research across various fields of medicine.<ref name=":3" /> Her work has included psychiatric research, cardiology, pediatrics, and other medical disciplines where behavioral factors play a significant role.<ref name=":3" /> Kraemer has contributed to methodologies aimed at addressing research problems where biological and behavioral interests converge, emphasizing the importance of measurement accuracy and the correction of errors in medical research.<ref name=":3" /> Kraemer’s research focuses on assessing the quality of measurements, including the evaluation of medical tests for reliability and validity.<ref name=":3" /> This work involves identifying potential sources of error in measurements, developing methods to detect these errors, and devising strategies for correcting them.<ref name=":3" /> Kraemer has examined the impacts of such errors on both clinical decision-making and scientific research outcomes.<ref name=":3" /> Her methodological contributions are aimed at improving the accuracy of research results and minimizing the risk of incorrect inferences.<ref name=":3" />

Kraemer has been involved in a broad range of medical research projects.<ref name=":3" /> These have included randomized clinical trials, epidemiological studies, prevention studies, and [[basic research]].<ref name=":3" /> In her work on clinical trials and other studies, Kraemer has been interested in issues related to statistical power, the ability of a study to detect an effect if one exists.<ref name=":3" /> She has researched strategies to improve statistical power not by increasing sample size, but through research design.<ref name=":3" /> Kraemer has also focused on training medical researchers and clinicians to recognize the challenges associated with drawing inferences from research results.<ref name=":3" /> She has emphasized the importance of understanding the limitations of research designs and methodologies, as well as the risks of making incorrect conclusions based on flawed or insufficient data.<ref name=":3" /> Kraemer's efforts in education and mentorship have aimed to equip researchers with the tools to critically assess the quality of their studies and improve the rigor of medical research.<ref name=":3" />

== Awards and honors ==
Kraemer became a fellow of the American Statistical Association in 1987. She is a member of the [[American College of Neuropsychopharmacology]] (1994) and the [[Institute of Medicine of the National Academies]] (2003).<ref name=":3" /> She was awarded the Franklin Ebaugh Prize from Stanford University and the Harvard Prize in Psychiatric Biostatistics and Epidemiology (2001).<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> In 2014, she was awarded an honorary degree from [[Wesleyan University]].<ref name=":2" />
